documentos.index_title: 1968 - LESBIAN PARTICIPATION IN THE 1968 STUDENT STRUGGLE
documentos.index_subtitle: Participation of the founder of the first lesbian feminist group, Marcela O. in the 1968 student struggle.
documentos.title: 1968 - LESBIAN PARTICIPATION IN THE 1968 STUDENT STRUGGLE
documentos.subtitle: In the student and popular struggle of 1968, there was also a significant lesbian participation, such as that of Marcela Olavarrieta, a radical anarchist separatist lesbian feminist, who founded the first Mexican feminist group of radical lesbian and heterosexual women in 1976.
paragraphs: On October 2, 1968, the historic student-popular massacre was perpetrated in Mexico by the Mexican army, ordered by the Minister of the Interior Luis Echeverría, one of the most repressive dictators of the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) during the Cold War, who was subsequently rewarded with the presidency of the republic from 1970 to 1976.

Days before said genocide, the predecessor of the Mexican lesbian-feminist movement, Marcela Olavarrieta, at barely 19 years old, was pursued by the military in her home state of Veracruz for simply distributing flyers. When they could not find her, they detained her father for interrogation for three days. Meanwhile, family and friends hid Marcela in the trunk of a car that transported her to Mexico City to protect her from political persecution in Veracruz. Consequently, being in hiding, she could not participate in the historic October 2 march, remembered as the night of the Tlatelolco massacre.

Marcela's crime was fighting for the democratization of education and the country; an end to repression against students; freedom for political prisoners; the dissolution of the brutal granaderos corps; and the demand for dialogue with the government—democratic demands to which the State responded with armed force. Since then, Marcela distinguished herself through her deep commitment to the struggle against the capitalist system and for the emancipation of indigenous peoples and women through her radical anarchist separatist feminism and, particularly, her lesbian feminism which would culminate eight years later, in 1976, in her lesbian feminist project, Ákratas.

Marcela was the one who planted the seed of radical feminism (RF) in Mexico, which would later confront liberal feminism (LF) that eventually proposed a 'feminism without women' and transformed into an enemy of women through genderist and queerist ideologies. Her radicalism kept her on the margins, but her praxis continues to be the guide for radical and lesbofeminist Mexican women.

documentos.index_title: 1977 - COMBAHEE RIVER COLLECTIVE STATEMENT
documentos.index_subtitle: One of the first black, lesbian, socialist, and third-world feminist groups in the US
documentos.title: 1977- COMBAHEE RIVER COLLECTIVE STATEMENT
documentos.subtitle: One of the first black, lesbian, socialist, and third-world feminist groups in the U.S.
paragraphs: Statement of principles published by the Combahee River Collective in April 1977 in Boston, one of the first black lesbian, socialist, and third-world feminist groups in the U.S. The collective split in 1974 from the National Black Feminist Organization (NBFO), the first liberal-oriented National Black Feminist Organization, as the Collective was much more radical, maintaining its work until 1980. Its political definition was anti-patriarchal, anti-racist, anti-imperialist, anti-capitalist, anti-lesbophobic, and situated as part of Third World women in the U.S. The Collective took its name from the guerrilla military action led by the enslaved black woman Harriet Tubman in 1863 on the blackwater Combahee River in South Carolina, U.S. Two of its most prominent founders were Barbara Smith and Demita Frazier.

For the Collective, categories of race and class, as well as sex, were intimately linked, but they criticized both the racism and classism of white intellectual feminism and the sexism of their black male comrades in struggle, without reaching the fragmentation promoted by white separatist organizations. The Combahee River Collective has been, and is, a powerful reference for black and socialist feminism, as well as for the entire anti-patriarchal, anti-racist, anti-imperialist, and anti-capitalist feminist struggle, being also very interesting for its self-location as part of Third World women (Africa, Asia, Latin America) within the United States itself.

The Combahee River Collective has been, and is, a powerful reference for black feminism, socialist feminism, and the entire anti-patriarchal, anti-racist, anti-imperialist, and anti-capitalist feminist struggle. It is very important that they identified as part of Third World women (Africa, Asia, Latin America) within the United States. As they said, if Black women were free, it would mean that everyone else would have to be free since our freedom would require the destruction of all systems of oppression.

documentos.index_title: 2021 - LESBOFEMINISM: BASIC NOTIONS
documentos.index_subtitle: Outstanding ideological-political contributions on lesbofeminism, lesbian separatism, and gynosocieties
documentos.title: 2021 - LESBOFEMINISM: BASIC NOTIONS
documentos.subtitle: Synthesis of the most outstanding ideological-political contributions on lesbofeminism, lesbian separatism, and gynosocieties.
paragraphs: Menstruadora, Luisa Velázquez Herrera, presents a historical journey through the most outstanding ideological-political contributions that have founded the notion of 'lesbofeminism,' against the historical alterations and conceptual manipulations carried out by misogynistic genderist, GLBT, and queer personalities and associations whose only objective is profit, academic prestige, or reaching positions of power.

Luisa analyzes the profound reflections of Adrienne Rich, Sheila Jeffreys, and many other authors on the deep political and revolutionary character of love between women, not reduced to sexual practice, particularly the essential contributions of Karina Vergara Sánchez.

Luisa explains that heterosexuality is the basis of the foundation of patriarchy and male domination, through the destruction of relationships between women. Its purpose is to force them to work for free for men and in favor of capitalism, which uses their exploitation through the sexual division of labor, subjecting each of them under the surveillance of an immediate man: husband, boyfriend, father, son, brother, neighbor, pimp, police officer, ruler, among others. This mechanism is not natural but created to make them believe that women were born to 'live alongside men.'

Lesbofeminism is any practice that, from political autonomy, seeks to free women from any bond to men imposed by the system, through lesbianhood and by lesbianizing the practice of women's liberation, building a collective lesbian existence with anti-racist and anti-colonialist foundations—a return to denied history. For this purpose, gynosocieties based on lesbian separatism are proposed as a utopia, recovering clitoral, vulvar, and uterine existence not for men, but for women themselves.

For lesbofeminism, trans and queer thought are theories and philosophical proposals cooked up in the neoliberal capitalism of the great hegemonies, aimed at denying and erasing the material reality of being women in order to tear apart their movement for liberation and resistance.

documentos.index_title: 1996 - AN EXPERIENCE WITHIN THE LESBIAN GROUPS OF MEXICO, 70s, LESBOS AND OIKABETH
documentos.index_subtitle: Synthesis article of the first six foundational years of the lesbian feminist movement 1977-1982.
documentos.title: 1996 - AN EXPERIENCE WITHIN THE LESBIAN GROUPS OF MEXICO, 70s, LESBOS AND OIKABETH
documentos.subtitle: Article presenting a synthesis of the first six years of struggle of the lesbian feminist movement in Mexico from 1977 to 1982, FEM magazine, 1996.
paragraphs: FEM MAGAZINE XX ANNIVERSARY. OCTOBER 1996. No. 163.

On its XX Anniversary, FEM, the most prestigious Mexican feminist magazine of the second half of the 20th century, published several articles by committed militants of the feminist movement who had been co-founders of the organizations that emerged in the 1970s with which the Mexican feminist movement began. They presented a brief description of each woman's experience in the development of these organizations and her analysis of achievements, progress, successes, and failures.

Marta Lamas wrote about her experience in MAS and MLM; Esperanza Brito on MNM; Eli Bartra on the La Revuelta Collective; Sonia Riquer on The Women's Collective (Trotskyist); Yan María C. and Luz María M. on lesbian groups: Lesbos and Oikabeth; Leticia Murúa on GAMU and Isabel Barranco on CAMVAC.

Yan María C. and Luz María M. wrote the article: An experience within the lesbian groups of Mexico, 70s, autonomist line Lesbos and Oikabeth, pages 26 to 32, in which they relate the development process of the first two lesbian feminist groups created in Mexico, Lesbos (1977) and Oikabeth I (1978). The article begins with the absolute repression lesbians experienced and continues with the difficulties they faced in organizing; their participation in the Feminist Women's Coalition (CMF) and the rejection by many heterosexual feminists; the first contacts with the homosexual groups FHAR and Lambda; the foundation with these groups of the CGH (Coordinator of Homosexual Groups) and the misogyny within it; the great rise of both the lesbian and socialist homosexual sex-political movement towards the end of the 70s; the decline of said movement and its fall; and finally, the end of Oikabeth I.

documentos.index_title: 1981 - AN ESSAY ON LESBIAN SEPARATISM, FEMINISM FIRST
documentos.index_subtitle: One of the deepest and clearest lesbian feminist analyses on the subject of lesbian separatism.
documentos.title: 1981 - FEMINISM FIRST, AN ESSAY ON LESBIAN SEPARATISM
documentos.subtitle: One of the deepest and clearest lesbian feminist analyses on the subject of lesbian separatism
paragraphs: This book began to be written by a collective of lesbians in 1978 in the US and was published in 1981 by Katharine Hess, Jean Langford, and Kathy Ross. It constituted, and still constitutes, a fundamental guide to clarifying mistaken or malicious interpretations on the subject of feminist-lesbian separatism. It conceives separatism not as an end, but as a tactic of struggle to combat patriarchy and build a strong feminist movement toward a great feminist revolution. It places feminism as a priority in the struggle of lesbians and questions heterosexuality for promoting the identification of women with men rather than with other women, hiding that men enjoy the benefit of women's oppression, whether they are heterosexual or homosexual.

The book performs a deep analysis of nationalist, territorial, racial, and class separatisms in social movements, as well as a critique of separatist proposals it considers incorrect, such as economic, 'separate,' matriarchalist, and extremist ones. It establishes a comparison with the other two strongest political positions of the feminist movement: radical feminism (RF) and socialist feminism (SF). It argues why separatist feminism must not 'separate' from the struggle against other social oppressions like colonialism, classism, and racism, including the rejection of Jews, ageism, and fatphobia, but always sustained by women's own feminist political autonomy.

This analysis distinguishes itself from other separatist proposals that lost their way in the marginalization of small groups separated from society and, above all, from social movements and struggles, which offered important contributions like community life and non-systemic lifestyles but were far removed from social reality.

documentos.index_title: 2009 - CENTRAL DOCUMENT OF THE VI LESBIAN-FEMINIST MARCH 2009, COMAL
documentos.index_subtitle: VI Lesbian Feminist March 2009, political positioning of the lesbian-feminist movement, COMAL.
documentos.title: 2009 - CENTRAL DOCUMENT OF THE VI LESBIAN-FEMINIST MARCH 2009
documentos.subtitle: Central document of the VI Lesbian Feminist March 2009 presenting the political position of the lesbian feminist movement gathered around COMAL (Lesbian March Committee), 2009.
paragraphs: This pronouncement constituted the Central Document of the VI LESBIAN FEMINIST MARCH OF 2009, read at the rally at its end, as the positioning of lesbian-feminists regarding world reality. It is important to insist that lesbian positions always include references to national and/or international realities from which the lesbian struggle cannot be detached. But this document in particular is an example of the critical analysis and commitment of lesbian feminists to said reality, unlike the sexual market which is alien to them, as well as the integral and global vision of lesbians, unlike the genitalized vision of sexual diversity.

The document states that lesbians as a political movement have been fighting for more than three decades for the transformation of the capitalist and neoliberal social economic organization model that has plunged peoples into debt, unemployment, and poverty, alongside energy and climate crises and militarization.

Therefore, it is urgent to abandon the dollar as a reference in international exchanges; to end export-oriented mono-production; to stop megaprojects that produce incalculable damage to indigenous and peasant peoples; to reject the WTO-imposed FTAs and SPP that lead to loss of autonomy; and to combat food dependency that prevents sustainable production and protection of biodiversity and traditional knowledge. It also rejects the presence of the Southern Command and 'anti-terrorist laws.'

And, of course, it denounces the criminalization of women in their struggle for the right to decide over their own bodies, demanding the legalization of abortion, fair treatment for lesbian women, and respect for diverse families.
documentos.footnote: * Proposal by Juana Guzmán Lisea, member of the Organizing Committee of the Lesbian March and the LesVOZ Organization, for the Central Document of the 2009 Lesbian March.

documentos.index_title: 1978 - PHOTOGRAPH AND CLARIFYING DOCUMENT “WHY MARCELA YES AND NANCY NO”
documentos.index_subtitle: Unpublished photograph of Marcela and Nancy and clarification of the deep political differences between them.
documentos.title: 1978 - CLARIFICATION DOCUMENT “WHY MARCELA YES AND NANCY NO”
documentos.subtitle: Unpublished photograph of Marcela Olavarrieta and Nancy Cárdenas at the First Gathering of Feminists and Lesbians, held in December 1978.
documentos.image_label:
PHOTOGRAPH OF MARCELA OLAVARRIETA AND
NANCY CÁRDENAS
paragraphs: This unpublished photograph shows Marcela Olavarrieta and Nancy Cárdenas at the First Gathering of Feminists and Lesbians organized by the Oikabeth organization and the Lesbos group, with the collaboration of the Ákratas group, in December 1978, at Nancy's house in Cuernavaca. Although both could establish a cordial friendship, they maintained great political differences. Marcela was the initiator of the feminist lesbian movement in Mexico and Nancy was the initiator of the gay homosexual movement in Mexico. Despite Nancy being cooperative and very friendly with lesbians, she considered the formation of a specifically lesbian movement apart from homosexuals to be a great political error, calling it separatist, exclusionary, and androphobic.

Marcela represented a radical anarchist separatist lesbian feminist stance; Nancy, conversely, represented a liberal conservative integrationist gay homosexual stance. For this reason, lesbians gradually abandoned their friendship with Nancy, and only gay-homosexual women continued that relationship. Most importantly, around Nancy and from her influence, the first 'gay women' groups in Mexico emerged, whose political approach would be totally different from that of 'lesbian women' but which would nonetheless constantly penetrate and influence the lesbian movement, causing much confusion.
Marcela is to lesbians what Nancy is to homosexuals; for this reason, although her historical role is recognized, she has by no means been a reference for the Mexican lesbian movement.

Attached to the photograph are the documents of two presentations, one from April 13, 2001, titled 'Why Marcela yes and Nancy no' and another from September 27, 2007, titled 'Why Yan yes and Nancy no' presented by Yan María Yaoyólotl. The photograph is property of the AHMLFM-YMY but the author is unknown.

documentos.index_title: 1982 - FIRST LESBIAN GROUP IN A STATE OF THE COUNTRY, LESBIANAS MORELENSES
documentos.index_subtitle: First lesbian organizational experience in the states of the Mexican republic, indigenous town of Ocotepec.
documentos.title: 1982 - FIRST LESBIAN GROUP IN A STATE OF THE MEXICAN REPUBLIC, LESBIANAS MORELENSES
documentos.subtitle: First lesbian feminist group in a state of the Mexican Republic, indigenous town of Ocotepec, state of Morelos, 1982-1987.
paragraphs: The first Mexican lesbian feminist organization in a state outside the capital was the group LESBIANAS MORELENSES (LM). This was a significant first considering that lesbophobic repression in the states was extremely more devastating, cruel, and brutal than in the capital. The group was founded in the indigenous town of Ocotepec, Cuernavaca, State of Morelos in May 1982 and concluded in 1987, spanning five and a half years of lesbian work. It also represented the first organization composed of popular, proletarian, and indigenous lesbian women. Furthermore, it constituted the first Mexican lesbian commune experience with self-sustaining intentions. Its political definition was socialist feminist lesbianism.

documentos.index_title: 1972 - RACE AND SEX, 1972: COLLISION OR COMRADERY?
documentos.index_subtitle: Essay by Radical Women of Seattle, Washington articulating: sex, class, race, and the Third World from socialist feminism.
documentos.title: 1972- RACE AND SEX, 1972: COLLISION OR COMRADERY?
documentos.subtitle: Radical Women (RWSW) solid proposal for articulating sex, class, race, and the Third World from revolutionary Socialist Feminism
paragraphs: Essay published in 1972 by Radical Women of Seattle, Washington (SWRW), written by Dorothy Mejia Chambless, a socialist feminist women's organization that emerged in 1969. Although the text does not directly touch on the subject of lesbianism, it offers one of the most complete and profound feminist proposals on the relationship between sex, class, and race, as well as the Third World (Africa, Asia, and Latin America) within the US, serving as a guide for Mexican socialist feminist lesbianism of the 1970s and 1980s.

SWRW was one of the most consistent organizations of revolutionary political radicalism. It proposed that the women's movement and the black movement should meet within the working-class movement under the leadership of radical third-world women for socialism. Therefore, they linked sex and race, as indicated by the essay title, but also class and the Third World. Simultaneously, they criticized the chauvinist and sexist practices of both white and black men participating in radical movements, as white men refused to support the women's liberation movement and many black men disparagingly called those militants of the black movement who also fought for female liberation 'matriarchs' and 'castrators.'

Women are objectively the connecting link between all sections of movements of the oppressed for social change; therefore, the alliance of black and white women is decisive. Women will determine the direction of the entire radical movement.

The article shows how from the beginning of the feminist movement in the 1970s, Afro-American women also began to organize, and likewise, white women's organizations began to emerge articulating the racial struggle, class struggle, sexual struggle, and also that of the Third World, refuting the false queer reduction of feminism as 'racist and classist.'

documentos.index_title: 2019 - WHERE IS PATRIARCHY?
documentos.index_subtitle: Lesbofeminism against patriarchal interpretations of “patriarchy” and “heteropatriarchy.”
documentos.title: 2019 - WHERE IS PATRIARCHY?
documentos.subtitle: Reflection refuting distorted and corrupt interpretations of the concepts “patriarchy/heteropatriarchy” to clarify, in light of lesbofeminism, the confusion intentionally created by genderism and queerism.
paragraphs: This 2019 text by Patricia Karina Vergara Sánchez offers a very precise and powerful interpretation of the concepts 'patriarchy' and 'heteropatriarchy' in light of lesbofeminism, so necessary and urgent to clarify the confusion that genderism and queerism have intentionally created around them.

It is worth remembering that after the great historical impact produced by the radical feminist movement (RFM) in the 1970s, the patriarchal system launched a counter-revolutionary offensive starting in the 80s to halt and disappear feminism, replacing it with genderism (gender ideology) and disparaging it as something that no longer had a reason to exist because women had supposedly already achieved what they sought and were now free.

Therefore, feminism was rendered unnecessary, backward, and obsolete compared to the 'wonderful achievements of genderism' (gender perspective). Consequently, one of the objectives was to invalidate one of the fundamental concepts of feminism, patriarchy, using neoliberal social sciences to demonstrate that said concept was invalid, groundless, and absurd.

However, despite institutional efforts to make it disappear, feminists continued to speak of patriarchy and to combat it. Therefore, since the 2000s, the neo-patriarchy changed strategy to appropriate this concept to neutralize it in light of genderist and queer theories, emptying it of content and depoliticizing it. Since then, misogynistic and lesbophobic patriarchal men, mainly from the social sciences, began to speak of 'patriarchy' and 'heteropatriarchy' but with a completely contradictory, misogynistic, and anti-feminist sense to confuse those who knew little or nothing about feminism.

documentos.index_title: 1997 - SECOND COALITION OF LESBIAN GROUPS IN MEXICO, ENLACE LÉSBICO
documentos.index_subtitle: Second network of lesbian organizations, after the first in 1987, the National Coordinator of Lesbians.
documentos.title: 1997 - SECOND COALITION OF LESBIAN GROUPS IN MEXICO, ENLACE LÉSBICO
documentos.subtitle: Second network of lesbian organizations in Mexico founded in 1997 (the first was CNL in 1987), it gathered ten groups to provide visibility to lesbians, fight for their rights, and against discrimination.
paragraphs: Enlace Lésbico (Lesbian Link) was the second network of Mexican lesbians, founded in 1997. It was born to unite, support, and provide presence to the lesbian sector, address their needs, and face the discrimination of the repressive policies of the System. It represented the second effort of the autonomous Mexican lesbian movement to build an organism to unite groupings fighting for lesbian liberation, constituting the continuation of the National Coordinator of Lesbians (CNL) formed in 1987 by twelve groups from the Mexican republic.

Enlace Lésbico had ten groups: Grumale II (Lesbian Mothers), Himen (Editor of LESVOZ magazine), Center for Documentation and Historical Archive of Lesbians (Lesbian Archive), Editorial CDAHL (Lesbian publisher), National Organization for the Human Rights of Lesbian Women (PRO-ML), Telemanita (Women Videographers) from Morelos, Nocturna-les (Young Poets), La Luna (Space for elderly lesbians) from Veracruz, Coyolxauhqui 'Z' (Lesbian women in visual arts), and Las Independientes (Lesbians who did not belong to any group).

Its objectives were: initiatives to solve the specific needs of lesbians; promoting visibility to gain public spaces; responding with a voice to the repression or discrimination they were subjected to; fighting for their civil, labor, health, housing, and political rights; and promoting lesbian culture.

It should be noted that in this second Mexican coalition of lesbian groups, Patria Jiménez's group, El Closet de Sor Juana, was not admitted for being a lesbo-gay, GLBT, queer group and not a lesbian group. Nevertheless, she continued to illegally claim representation of Mexican lesbians before government institutions and international organizations along with her partner Gloria Careaga.

documentos.index_title: 1970 - LESBIANISM: A SOCIALIST FEMINIST PERSPECTIVE
documentos.index_subtitle: Written by Susan Williams, from the socialist feminist organization Radical Women of Seattle, Washington.
documentos.title:
1970 - LESBIANISM: A SOCIALIST FEMINIST PERSPECTIVE
by Susan Williams, Radical Women Seattle, Washington
documentos.subtitle: One of the foundational documents of socialist feminist lesbianism as part of the struggle of working women, radical women, and the socialist proposal
paragraphs: This text constitutes one of the first fundamental analyses of socialist feminism (SF) on the subject of lesbianism at the beginning of the 1970s. Unfortunately, it reached the hands of the Oikabeth organization only in the early 80s, a time when in Mexico the feminist movement was being inexorably diverted by genderism (gender focus), thus losing the opportunity to strengthen and extend the proposal of Radical Women of Seattle in the country and Latin America.

The text explains that lesbians, in addition to fighting against a sexist society that considered lesbianism a disease, also had to fight against the machismo of homosexual organizations of liberal middle-class gay men; against the denial of lesbianism within white, heterosexual liberal feminist groups; and finally, against the left for its ambiguity regarding women. For these reasons, many radicalized lesbians sought refuge in separatism. The origin of said sexism emerged when men appropriated the 'surplus' of social production as their property and base of power; therefore, male domination is not the result of any innate biological or mental superiority, but a product of: private property, wealth accumulation, and its transmission through the paternal line, parallel to the isolation of women from social production and their reduction to 'wives' and 'mothers.'

Lesbians challenge sexist social rules and are thus persecuted, facing a double oppression: as women and as lesbians. If they are also a racial or ethnic minority, workers, or poor, their oppression triples or quadruples. Therefore, social liberation can only be achieved through the union of all oppressed groups, recognizing their specific oppressions in the synergy (joint work) of their class, race, and sex struggles. Working women are the ones who connect these separate struggles, which qualifies them for revolutionary leadership. Capitalism cannot eradicate sexism, racism, poverty, war, or labor exploitation because it is based on them; the only liberation is through a socialist revolution. The transformation of lesbianism into a revolutionary force requires a socialist feminist analysis.

documentos.index_title: 2017 - COMMITTEE, ZAPATISTA LESBIANS IN SUPPORT OF INDIGENOUS WOMAN FOR THE PRESIDENCY
documentos.index_subtitle: Support for indigenous Nahua comrade Marichuy for the presidency of the Mexican republic by CNI and EZLN.
documentos.title: 2017 - ZAPATISTA LESBIAN COMMITTEE IN SUPPORT OF INDIGENOUS WOMAN FOR THE PRESIDENCY OF THE REPUBLIC
documentos.subtitle: This communique from the Zapatista Lesbian Feminist Committee (CLFZ) declares its unconditional support for the candidacy for the presidency of the Mexican republic of the indigenous woman of Nahua origin María del Jesús Patricio, Marichuy.
paragraphs: This communique from the Zapatista Lesbian Feminist Committee (CLFZ) declares its unconditional support for the candidacy for the presidency of the Mexican republic of the indigenous woman of Nahua origin María del Jesús Patricio, Marichuy, proposed by the National Indigenous Congress (CNI) and the Zapatista Army of National Liberation (EZLN). It also joins the Political Program proposed by the Indigenous Governing Council (CIG) to build a just future for Mexico.

The members of the Committee have a history of supporting the EZLN struggle since 1994, participating in the Sixth Declaration, and supporting the defense of indigenous nations and peasant struggles against racism, dispossession, and genocide. For this reason, they explicitly distance themselves from merchant and mercenary groupings (NGOs) that call themselves 'lesbians' or 'lesbian feminists' exclusively to access national and international funding and/or government positions.

Imperialist, classist, racist, and sexist postmodern theorists have accused indigenous nations, as well as women, the proletariat, and nature itself, of being 'purists,' 'fundamentalists,' and 'essentialists' for not submitting to the techno-scientific economic-political control of capital. They attack the originality (the origin), authenticity, and historicity of these social sectors to seize their territory, bodies, natural resources, wisdom, etc., abolishing their traditions, organizational forms, autonomous spaces, community governments, and natural resources, which constitutes a form of genocide.

The communique reminds us that lesbian feminists identify with indigenous nations because just as they have faced marginalization, dispossession, and repression, we as women in rebellion, lesbians, have also suffered marginalization, dispossession, and repression. Attacks perpetrated by a common enemy: savage capitalist patriarchy, currently called neoliberal globalization.

documentos.index_title: 2018 - BOOK: LESBOFEMINISM FOR WHAT
documentos.index_subtitle: The struggle of six lesbofeminist militants against compulsory heterosexuality as a weapon of patriarchy.
documentos.title: 2018 - BOOK: LESBOFEMINISM FOR WHAT
documentos.subtitle: This book presents the experience and reflection of six militants of the Mexican lesbofeminist movement, covering topics from women's communities, resistance, women as a class, and separatism to the critique of compulsory heterosexuality, genderism, and the misogynistic character of gayism, toward the proposal of a new lesbofeminist society.
paragraphs: This book presents the experience and reflection of six militants of Mexican lesbofeminism.

- Patricia Karina Vergara Sánchez in “Why and for what do we lesbofeminists fight?” speaks about the lesbofeminist utopia, explaining that the daily reality of murders, injuries, deaths, and abductions of women, along with the heavy workloads of service, procreation, and unpaid care, constructs them as a class. Therefore, lesbofeminism represents the alliance of women in rebellion, ceasing to serve the class of men, based on separatism against the political regime of compulsory heterosexuality.

- Luisa Velázquez Herrera -menstruadora- in For what does lesbofeminism fight?, from a millennial lesbianism, lesbofeminism pursues the end of patriarchy. In the past, men imposed themselves over the communal life of women through violence, appropriating them to exploit them through compulsory heterosexuality and forcing them to be their 'complement.' Lesbofeminism is the resistance of the community of women caring for and loving each other for a dignified world for them; this is to 'lesbianize' oneself.

- Yan María Castro Yaoyólotl in “Why and for what do we lesbian feminists fight”, describes how the lesbian movement laid its foundations in the 1970s and from the beginning criticized the misogynistic character of homosexuality and gayness; in the 90s it faced genderism; in the 2000s it proposed Lesbian-feminism against gay and GLBT commercialization; and in the 2010s as lesbofeminism it distanced itself from sexual diversity. Currently, it faces queerism, an expression of postmodern neoliberal globalization, a neo-patriarchy disguised as woman.

- Kitzia Montiel in “The best-kept secret”: for her, the best-kept secret was hiding the possibility of experiencing lesbianism. Coming from the GLBT world immersed in alcohol, violence, and misogyny, and a colonizing theory of 'gender' that by replacing women with gender hid the genocide against them, currently intending to strip them of their being women. But she finally found a communal space only for radical separatist lesbofeminist moon women.

- Evelyn M. Rodríguez in “Here I stay, from here I am: of the we”, considers heterosexuality as the root of oppression of women and separatist lesbofeminism as resistance to the patriarchal world. Since she was a child, she tried to understand who she was through a difficult process of searching. She proposes the depatriarchalization of all forms of dispossession, violation, and expropriation of women through separation—that is, ceasing to serve men—alongside the construction of a fabric among ourselves.
- PV in “She”. Narrates the story of her mother at 66 years old, never being able to live her lesbianism openly, remaining in the most absolute silence.

documentos.index_title: 2007 - LESBIAN-FEMINIST MARCH 2007 and XXX ANNIVERSARY OF THE MOVEMENT (1977-2007)
documentos.index_subtitle: March organized by Left Lesbian Feminists against neoliberalism and the XXX Anniversary of the movement.
documentos.title:
2007 - CENTRAL DOCUMENT OF THE LESBIAN-FEMINIST MARCH 2007,
XXX ANNIVERSARY OF THE LESBIAN-FEMINIST MOVEMENT (1977)
documentos.subtitle: Central document of the 2007 Lesbian Feminist March organized by Left Lesbian-Feminists, on the XXX anniversary of the foundation of the Lesbian Feminist Movement in Mexico. It exposes a critique of neoliberal economic policies at the national level, including the devastating sexual diversity market, and manifests its leftist positioning.
paragraphs: XXX ANNIVERSARY OF THE FOUNDATION OF THE LESBIAN-FEMINIST MOVEMENT IN MEXICO 1977 – 2007

The Lesbian-Feminist Movement began in 1977, and its historical-political importance in 2007 lay in the fact that repression against lesbians had not decreased but intensified through pauperization, unemployment, job instability, the uncontrollable increase in femicide, and intra- and extra-domestic violence imposed by neoliberalism, to which lesbophobia was added.

The lesbian-feminist movement claimed feminism as its political guide against patriarchy toward the liberation of women from sexual slavery (which did not interest gays because precisely the Sexual Diversity Market was sustained by it). Establishing, from its political autonomy, alliances with women's and feminist movements, as well as with anti-patriarchal and leftist homosexuals, bisexuals, transgender, and transsexuals.

Feminist lesbianism marked a sharp difference from gay-homosexual women, GLBT, queer, and trans-people and neoliberal genderists. It criticized Gay Parades or GLBT Carnivals because they abandoned the initial principles that gave rise to marches and the lesbian-homosexual movement in Mexico, denouncing that capitalist companies had taken over these carnivals. Unlike the GLBT, lesbian feminists did not intend to 'fit in,' 'adapt,' or 'integrate' into the system through the search for 'civil rights,' 'citizenship,' and 'extension of privileges,' but sought to end and liquidate it through a radical change in economic, political, social, and sexual structures toward the construction of a new social organization without human oppression or exploitation.

The Lesbian-Feminist March did not constitute a lucrative business, but the continuation of the political work of lesbians against electoral fraud, the criminalization of social struggles (Atenco, Oaxaca, and Chiapas), the sale of the country to multinationals through FTAs, the privatization of resources and companies belonging to the Mexican people, the invasion of GMOs, the privatization of water, and the theft of germplasm and endemic species that accelerated the impoverishment of indigenous and peasant communities, as well as against the devastating control of the Sexual Diversity Market.

documentos.title: 1970 - “THE WOMAN-IDENTIFIED WOMAN” FOUNDATIONAL MANIFESTO OF THE LESBIAN FEMINIST MOVEMENT BY RADICALESBIANS
documentos.subtitle: “The Woman-Identified Woman” constitutes the first foundational manifesto of the lesbian feminist movement in the US, published by RadicaLesbians in 1970.
paragraphs: The Woman-Identified Woman constitutes the foundational text of the lesbian feminist movement in the US, published by RadicaLesbians with the collective participation of Rita Mae Brown, Artemis March, Lois Hart, Ellen Shumsky, Cynthia Funk, and Karla Jay in 1970. This Manifesto maintains its current relevance against the offensive of the neoliberal postmodern queer phallopatriarchy that is promoting the disappearance of women.

The Manifesto was distributed during the famous Lavender Menace protest at the start of the Second Congress to Unite Women held in New York City, US, on May 1, 1970. The action was carried out by the RadicaLesbians group wearing t-shirts with the legend 'The Lavender Menace,' referring to the assertion by the NOW co-founder who warned against the lavender menace of lesbians, who in response took over the platform and the speakers' microphone protesting their exclusion. The RadicaLesbians stated that lesbians were at the forefront of the struggle for women's liberation because their identification with other women challenged the patriarchal imposition of female identity as 'men's sexual companions'; therefore, the commitment to lesbian liberation was essential for the success of the women's liberation movement.

Until women can see in each other the possibility of a primary commitment that includes sexual love, they will be denying themselves the love and value they give to men, thus affirming their second-class status. As long as the most important thing for them is acceptance by men individually as well as politically, the term lesbian will be used against women effectively. As long as they seek only more privileges within the (patriarchal) system, they will not want to antagonize the power of men.

documentos.index_title: 2017 - NOTE FOR THE FEMINIST WHO WANTS US ALL TO BE ONE AND THE SAME
documentos.index_subtitle: Critique of genderism and liberal feminism by Menstruadora, Luisa Velázquez Herrera.
documentos.title: 2017 - NOTE FOR THE FEMINIST WHO WANTS US ALL TO BE ONE AND THE SAME
documentos.subtitle: Published by La Crítica on May 08, 2017, by Luisa Velázquez Herrera, Menstruadora.
paragraphs: Feminism does not seek equality; liberal feminism, located in patriarchal institutions such as academia, media, governments, NGOs, etc., is what seeks it. Liberal feminists seek half of the exploitation pie: to become business owners, deputies, academics, and presidents who will speak of 'parity' and 'equity' without questioning or wanting to modify the patriarchal system. The pinnacle of liberal feminism, or its synonym, is the gender perspective, which does not come from women's struggle but from a discourse created by neoliberalism. It shifted from speaking of patriarchy to the sex-gender system, and from feminism to gender, eliminating the analysis of men's appropriation of women denounced by autonomous feminists and lesbofeminists. Behind the gender perspective discourse, forced sterilizations, sexual exploitation, 'empowerment,' and 'surrogacy'—promoted by liberals and postmoderns along with gay men, heterosexual men, and capitalist gay women—were hidden.

Fortunately, others, such as lesbofeminists and radical feminists, affirm that all oppressions have a material basis; being a woman is living in a sexed body with a uterus, vulva, and breasts, educated to serve men within a system hierarchical by social class and racial categorizations. The analysis of oppression does not seek to leave us stagnant but to face the power of men with knowledge of its origins and characteristics. Liberal and postmodern feminists are up in power working for men and will do everything possible to sell every piece of our bodies. It is no historical coincidence that there is so much talk of 'non-binary gender,' unicorns, and 'trans women'; there are organizations inflated with resources and juicy funding to promote an agenda that includes 'new masculinities,' 'surrogacy,' and 'sex work.'

That is the feminism we had to learn—postmodern neoliberal feminism. Those of us born in the eighties, nineties, and two-thousands are generations educated under the gender perspective/gender studies. In universities, they made us read Paul Preciado, Judith Butler, Despentes, and any follower of Foucault; that is why today it costs us so much to question their dogmas.

documentos.index_title: 1985 - LESBIAN FEMINIST MARXIST LENINIST SEMINAR AND THE SEAMSTRESSES' UNION
documentos.index_subtitle: Socialist lesbian participation in the creation and structuring of the first feminist workers' union.
documentos.title:
1985 - A lesbian expression in the proletarian movement
Lesbian Feminist Marxist Leninist Seminar (SMLFL)
documentos.subtitle: Struggle of lesbian feminists with women workers in the garment industry in the formation of their union
paragraphs: After the earthquake that shook Mexico City on September 19, 1985, the Lesbian Feminist Marxist Leninist Seminar (SMLFL) decided to support the garment workers who were outside the collapsed factories. Many workers died, and these seamstresses were asking only for the payment of their last week worked. We set up a camp next to the rubble and began the struggle. They had never organized, yet we faced the boss, the corrupt union representatives, and the army itself, and we went one step further by demanding full compensation for years worked.

For the first time, the seamstresses stopped being just housewives and child caregivers to become energetic fighters. The camp for many months became our second home, and it was there that we presented the lesbian feminist group, achieving a beautiful sisterhood overcoming all prejudices against lesbianism. Later, with other organizations that joined the struggle, we began to form the September 19 Seamstresses Union, with a feminist orientation.

Unfortunately, the discrimination did not come from the seamstresses but from a women's organization that argued the government would not grant registration to the union if it found out about the presence of a group of 'deviates' (lesbians), so we left the union. But our hearts remained with them, proving that prejudices are eliminated when we fight together.

documentos.index_title: 1987 - FIRST COALITION OF LESBIAN GROUPS, NATIONAL COORDINATOR OF LESBIANS (CNL)
documentos.index_subtitle: The CNL, first alliance of twelve lesbian groups to fight against general oppression and for their civil rights.
documentos.title: 1987 - FIRST COALITION OF LESBIAN GROUPS IN MEXICO, NATIONAL COORDINATOR OF LESBIANS (CNL)
documentos.subtitle: CNL Brochure (1st Ed.) For the first time in Mexico, twelve lesbian groups united, overcoming their dispersion in a coalition to fight against different forms of repression and for their civil, labor, health, child custody, housing, and security rights, in connection with other social movements.
paragraphs: The National Coordinator of Lesbians was formed in November 1987 with twelve lesbian groups—two of which were mixed heterosexual and lesbian women CIDHAL and Cuarto Creciente. The groups were: Patlatonalli Lesbian Group of Guadalajara, Lesbian Mothers, Lesbian Group of San Luis Potosí, Gestación Collective, Lesbians of Querétaro, Lesbian-Homosexual Group of Veracruz, Revolutionary Socialist Feminist Front of Guadalajara, Lesbianas Morelenses, CIDHAL, Cuarto Creciente, Lesbian Group of Tijuana, and Lesbian Feminist Marxist Leninist Seminar. Neither the Mula group nor Patria Jiménez's Oikabeth III group were included in the CNL.

The objectives of the CNL were: to promote the organization of different lesbian and lesbian feminist groups in the country to form a national movement; to fight for their rights regarding work, education, health, motherhood, child custody, housing, and social security; to reclaim their sexuality as women and as lesbians; to combat myths by providing scientific and objective information and dissemination about lesbianism; to fight against all types of sexism, classism, imperialism, racism, and interventionism and for the defense of human rights against repression based on sex, race, social class, political position, age, or religion; to support democratic, independent, and revolutionary organizations of different social sectors fighting against exploitation and oppression; to defend homosexual rights, fight against AIDS, and combat yellow journalism.
The CNL would be active from 1987 to 1991.

It should be noted that this first Mexican coalition of lesbian groups did not include the Mula group, which would disappear shortly after. Nor did it include Patria Jiménez's group, Oikabeth III, who, despite this, illegally claimed representation of Mexican lesbians before government institutions and international organizations through the lesbo-gay initiative, later LGBT and finally LGBTTTIQ+.

documentos.title: 2022 - LESBOFEMINIST ZAPOTEC INDIGENOUS POETRY, YADIRA DEL MAR
documentos.subtitle: Love between women as part of the self-affirmation of indigenous lesbians.
paragraphs: Art is an expression of the collective experience of the world; therefore, art is a reflection of the experiences and expectations of peoples. In this case, of indigenous peoples and lesbofeminist women's communities—a difficult and painful experience in a triple sense: being women in a misogynistic world; being lesbians in a heterosexist environment; and being indigenous in a racist and ethno-exclusionary context. Creating art in this framework is an expression that requires talent but, above all, a deep commitment to social struggles and a deep love for the community. Yadira shares this passion with us.

In the midst of a world that denies all identities other than those imposed by the neoliberal system, the survival of indigenous cultural identities represents a superhuman effort not to disappear, just as we women find ourselves fighting also not to disappear under neo-patriarchy. Both struggles merge in Yadira's poetry which, through lesbian love between women, expresses the clear and firm political position of radical feminism.

documentos.index_title: 1996 - CO-OPTATION OF FEMINISM BY PATRIARCHY
documentos.index_subtitle: Co-optation of feminism through NGOs and gender technocracy: institutional feminism. By María Galindo.
documentos.title: 1996 - THE CO-OPTATION OF FEMINISM BY PATRIARCHY THROUGH NGOS, GENDER TECHNOCRACY, AND INSTITUTIONAL FEMINISM
documentos.subtitle: The importance of this text, presented in 1996 at the VII Latin American Feminist Gathering in Chile by María Galindo from Bolivia, titled “Sabotaged time in which it is our turn to live,” lies in its precise and didactic exposure of the process of co-optation of feminism by patriarchy through NGOs and gender technocracy, resulting in “institutional feminism” or genderism, which took charge of institutionalizing the concept: gender perspective.
paragraphs: The critique of the process of appropriation of feminism by patriarchy through NGOs, gender technocracy, and institutional feminism began to be questioned by the feminist collective Las Cómplices (mainly Margarita Pisano, Ximena Bedregal, and Edda Gaviola) in 1992 and presented in a paper at the VI Latin American Feminist Gathering in El Salvador in 1993.

In the following years, Las Cómplices managed to gather other feminists from Latin America who were also dissatisfied with the direction Latin American feminism was taking, until said critique was expressed jointly in 1996 at the VII Latin American Feminist Gathering in Chile.

The contributions of Las Cómplices (who would constitute the basis for the formation of Autonomous Feminism in Latin America) are indispensable for understanding how (liberal) feminism transformed into genderism, and later into queerism.

One of the papers presented in Chile '96 by one of the dissatisfied feminists was María Galindo's from Bolivia, “Sabotaged time in which it is our turn to live,” where in its first part, she exposed a very clear and didactic description for understanding how feminism was being co-opted by patriarchy and transformed into genderism. That first part of the paper is taken up, but without ignoring that she herself subsequently oriented toward queerism, abandoning lesbianism and feminism, because queerism is essentially anti-feminist.

The new neo-patriarchal political categories specified in the paper are:
  • - the category of gender or rhetoric from power: the gender perspective;
  • - institutionalized and bureaucratized feminism;
  • - gender technocracy;
  • - NGOs and NGO networks as the new organizational expression of said technocracy;
  • - the colonialist character of the funding agencies that nourish NGOs; and
  • - formal democracy in substitution of social movements.

These categories would serve to identify the so-called institutional feminism (later termed: genderism) that sold out to Northern (imperialist) funding agencies and local governments to enter and become part of institutionalization, reach government positions, and access international organizations, which would constitute gender technocracy.

documentos.title: 2012 - HERETIC DIFFUSION, LESBOFEMINIST EDITIONS ARGENTINA PUBLISHES COUNTER-HEGEMONIC MATERIALS
documentos.subtitle: Heretic Diffusion disseminates anti-capitalist and anti-patriarchal lesbofeminist documents promoting critical reflection and deep analysis to radicalize the feminist struggle.
paragraphs: Independent Lesbofeminist Editions of Buenos Aires, Argentina, in its editorial Ojo de Bruja (Witch's Eye) specifies that it is an autonomous lesbian initiative to circulate counter-hegemonic feminist materials: anti-capitalist, lesbian, radical, anti-racist, ecofeminist, anarchist, of feminist theories not disseminated or disappeared facing a patriarchal liberal context, betting that critical reflection and deep analysis generate radicalization of the feminist struggle, its self-criticism, and search for its identity, rescuing one's own words, thought, and herstory.

“Women with the liberation of women have understood the importance of having gatherings and other events solely for women. It is clear that dealing with men divides us and wastes our energies; it is not the job of the oppressed to explain their oppression to the oppressor. Women will also see that collectively men will not deal with their sexism until they are forced to. Even so, many of those same women continue to have primary relationships with individual men and do not understand why lesbians find that oppressive. Lesbians cannot grow politically or personally in a situation where the basis of our politics is denied: that lesbianism is political and that in heterosexuality the maintenance of Male Supremacy is crucial.”
The editorial claims to be anti-commercial and anti-copyright with the cry: intellectual property is theft! therefore it invites women to disseminate all its materials.

documentos.index_title: 1996 - DECLARATION OF AUTONOMOUS FEMINISM
documentos.index_subtitle: Declaration read at the VII Latin American Feminist Gathering, Chile 1996, by the Autonomous Feminism current.
documentos.title: 1996 - DECLARATION OF AUTONOMOUS FEMINISM VII LATIN AMERICAN AND CARIBBEAN FEMINIST GATHERING
documentos.subtitle:
Cartagena, November 26, 1996
Declaration read at the VII Latin American and Caribbean Feminist Gathering in 1996 by the political current of Autonomous Feminists.
paragraphs: For Autonomous Feminists, the feminist movement represents the union between the intimate, the private, and the public, without which it is incomplete—an articulation that allows the creation of a proposal for another culture, a dialogue with the social world that challenges patriarchal power in public and private and questions the State and its institutions in a critical process of rethinking the world. The legitimacy of the movement is not built by responding to the legality of the system, not in legal recognition by the State but in social practice.

We must invent the society we want to build, unite the manual and intellectual, recreate the subversive language that feminism initiated, recognize the contributions from autonomous feminist spaces that have developed outside the official spaces of institutionalization, and prevent our theoretical products from being used as monetary exchanges for legitimacy and institutional careers. And let the media amplify the voice to enrich thought and practice and not to create thinking and writing elites.

We must define the ethical limits of resources, instances, and methods and stop endorsing funding policies that deconstruct our democracy and thought and install themselves in every space that attempts to be rebellious. We refuse to negotiate with supranational and national institutions that cause hunger and misery, such as the Inter-American Development Bank, the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, etc. We must question the limits of money, of international cooperation, knowing and decoding the origin of its procedures, interpellate money and its power; we require our own resources with new practices to obtain and multiply them that do not depend on development cooperation.

We seek exchange with rebellious European and US women who question everything outside the definition of legitimacy given by political and academic power. Autonomy defines our relationship with the world, where we deepen our critique of the system and where we install our daily subversion based on our history and on relations of respect and visibility.
documentos.footnote: Declaration published in 1997 in Colección Feminismos Cómplices, Ed. La Correa Feminita, Centro de Investigación y Capacitación de la Mujer A. C., <cite>Permanencia voluntaria en la utopía.</cite>

documentos.index_title: 1997 - VOLUNTARY PERMANENCE IN UTOPIA
documentos.index_subtitle: The split of the feminist movement into: autonomous feminism and institutional feminism
documentos.title: 1997 - BOOK: VOLUNTARY PERMANENCE IN UTOPIA, AUTONOMY IN THE VII LATIN AMERICAN AND CARIBBEAN FEMINIST GATHERING, CHILE '96. 1997
documentos.subtitle: The split of the feminist movement into: autonomous feminism and institutional feminism
paragraphs: <cite>Colección Feminismos Cómplices. Ediciones del Taller Editorial La Correa Feminista, Centro de Investigación y Capacitación de la Mujer A. C., 1997.</cite>

This book offers the papers presented at the VII EFLAC in which the following participated: María Galindo “Sabotaged time in which it is our turn to live”; Elizabeth Álvarez “Conversing among ourselves”; Ximena Bedregal “Thinking in a new way”; Margarita Pisano “From my other corner”; Julieta Paredes “The hidden, the invisibilized”. The dialogue workshop for deepening Autonomous Feminism and its Declaration of Autonomous Feminism. Reflections on the Gathering by: Marta Fontenla and Magul Bellotti; Ochy Curiel and Yuderkys Espinoza; Julieta Paredes, Julieta Ojeda, and María Galindo; Patricia Kolesnikov and Olga Viglieca; Edda Gaviola Artigas; María Elena Bartís. And critique of press misinformation: letters from Margarita Pisano, Edda Gaviola, Marta Fontenla, and Magui Bellotti; Patricia Kolesnikov and Olga Viglieca; Olga Viglieca and Judith Gordon.

It is a book of reflections of the autonomous feminist (AF) current that formed the organizing committee of the VII EFLAC, whose fundamental objective was to strengthen the feminist movement and its political autonomy. But many 'empowered' women from NGOs tried to invalidate it through a smear campaign and economic and misinformation boycotts.

Autonomous feminism argued that it was necessary to identify the various forms of thought, practices, and interests within the movement, from those who defended the neoliberal system seeking “greater equity between the sexes” to smooth its sharpest edges without touching the deep bases of said system (those who allowed the emergence of a gender technocracy that gave rise to institutional feminism), to the feminists who questioned the deep logics of the patriarchal phallocentric hierarchical and linear macro-cultural system upon which sexism, racism, homophobia, violence, war, ecological predation, immeasurable wealth, and extreme poverty were built.

Feminism was in an accelerated process of institutionalization, mediated by negotiations with funding agencies and lobbies, speaking in the name of “all” and contravening feminist rebellion. The powers that Women's Networks had acquired were not neutral; they were achieving the demobilization and paralysis of the movement. Autonomous feminism proposed the delimitation of sponsors (institutions and International Cooperation Agencies) without interference in the political, methodological, and organizational decisions of feminist gatherings, respecting their autonomy. Gatherings were to be a moment for evaluating the policies and strategies carried out by the movement to project the future.

It should be noted that the majority of autonomous feminists were lesbians, despite not recognizing it as their central political position, which substantially influenced their vision of feminism and the defense of autonomy.

documentos.index_title: 2004 - LESBOFEMINISM REGARDING OPPRESSIVE SOCIALIZATION SPACES
documentos.index_subtitle: Development of the lesbian feminist struggle in non-oppressive spaces: clubs, bars, discos, and parties.
documentos.title:
2004 - LESBOFEMINISM REGARDING OPPRESSIVE SOCIALIZATION SPACES:
CLUBS, BARS, DISCOS, AND PARTIES
documentos.subtitle:
Talk with young gay people from Chilpancingo, Hidalgo Park, May 2004, Gloria Elia Salas.
Extract from the article: Lesbofeminists regarding liberating or oppressive spaces, by Luisa Margarita R.
paragraphs: “You are the space where you move” indicates that the physical space where we move, where all our activities, dynamics, behaviors, and social relations develop, can be constructive or destructive, liberating or oppressive. Oppressive spaces are designed by the patriarchal system to promote the consumption of alcohol, drugs, tobacco, junk food, gambling, exacerbated sex, the play of masculinity/femininity stereotypes, and oppressive and violent sex-affective relationships, which generate a lot of money for capitalists and are part of the social control machinery of capitalism.

HOMOSEXUAL OR GAY WOMEN = ALCOHOL = DRUGS = STEREOTYPES = VIOLENT SEX. Before the appearance of the lesbian movement in Mexico in 1976, clubs and bars were the only spaces for non-heterosexual women. Therefore, one of the first actions of the lesbian feminist movement was to take those women out of those club, bar, and disco spaces, providing them with healthy, positive, safe, and constructive alternatives to hold workshops, courses, retreats, teamwork, including social gatherings, dances, covens, and parties without alcohol, without drugs, exacerbated-compulsive sex, or sexual stereotypes. Homosexual-gay women opposed lesbians for offering healthy spaces, rejecting them as “moralistic,” “repressive,” “inhibiting,” “deniers of pleasure,” and “anti-sex” initiatives.

documentos.index_subtitle: The Lesbian Collective of Barcelona joined the Gay Liberation Front of Catalonia (FAGC) in 1977 and separated in 1978.
documentos.title: 1978 - SEPARATION OF THE LESBIAN COLLECTIVE OF BARCELONA FROM THE GAY LIBERATION FRONT OF CATALONIA (FAGC) IN 1978
documentos.subtitle: The Lesbian Collective of Barcelona joined the Gay Liberation Front of Catalonia (FAGC) in 1977 and separated in 1978, for reasons similar to those that induced Mexican lesbian feminist organizations of the 1970s never to join the homosexual movement (except Oikabeth for three months).
paragraphs: The Lesbian Collective within the FAGC, taking into account that male homosexuality is not free from machista influences, considered it necessary to introduce a Lesbian Collective to highlight machista manifestations and contradictions at every turn and introduce a constant debate on feminism and lesbianism. But internal evolution sharpened the male homosexual / lesbian woman contradiction because the oppression of the lesbian stems originally from the fact of being a woman, and therefore her struggle passes through the feminist struggle. Hence, becoming independent from the FAGC, it defines its revolutionary space alongside women within the Feminist Movement, as their oppression and the path to follow for their liberation is common.

documentos.index_title: 2022 - SIWAPAJTI, WOMAN'S MEDICINE. MEMORY AND THEORY OF WOMEN
documentos.index_subtitle: Recovery of physical, corporal, and symbolic territories seized by patriarchy.
documentos.title:
2022 - Siwapajti, Woman's Medicine.
Memory and Theory of Women
documentos.subtitle: Patriarchal society was consolidated by breaking the bonds between women through compulsory heterosexuality; their traditions and ancestral knowledge were criminalized and appropriated by men of science. The recovery of these physical, corporal, and symbolic territories, traditions, and memories is the banner of struggle for women. This book by Karina is an invitation to the insubordination of women.
paragraphs: Siwapajti is a necessary book for every Latin American woman seeking to understand the roots of the patriarchal world-system, an indispensable task for developing forceful strategies to face, overthrow, and suffocate the femicidal dominance of men. Karina shares a succinct and eloquent explanation of how this system has been shaped through the centuries, from Mesoamerican times, through colonization, to capitalism and its current neoliberal phase. Her explanation leaves no doubt about how men's power has been entirely intentional to counteract women's inevitable radiance and how to achieve this they have imposed on us the regime of heterosexuality, which has sustained the economic models of patriarchy as its backbone.

Siwapajti is that explanation we were looking for when first arriving at feminism and which no one could offer us in the monopoly of genderists, always so collaborationist with men; it is the explanation we exhaled in our moments of rage when defending ourselves from men's harassment and it is also what we feel in moments of immense love among ourselves in the heat of hope. Siwapajti is a splash of truth about a path we already knew how to walk; it is a book born to be passed from hand to hand, from mouth to mouth, between lesbians' kisses—even those who are not yet—to remind women of the rebellion we will become again.

documentos.title: 2011 - MARISELA ESCOBEDO, A SYMBOL OF THE STRUGGLE AGAINST FEMICIDE AND IMPUNITY
documentos.subtitle: Denunciation by the group, Lesbians of the feminist movement against femicide, against the murder of activist Marisela Escobedo occurring on December 16, 2010, victim of femicide for the act of seeking justice for the femicide of her daughter Rubí Marisol occurring in 2008.
paragraphs: The group, Lesbians of the feminist movement against femicide, denounced on the Day Against Violence toward Women, November 25, 2011, the government of Chihuahua and particularly Governor César Duarte Jáquez for the impunity prevailing in his government that allowed an uncontrollable killing of women without being stopped. The feminist movement was shocked by the murder of activist Marisela Escobedo on December 16, 2010, victim of femicide for the act of seeking justice for the femicide of her daughter Rubí Marisol in 2008.

In 2008 Rubí Frayre Escobedo, Marisela's 16-year-old daughter, was murdered in Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, by her partner, Sergio Rafael Barraza. Despite the murderer himself confessing to the crime, even indicating where he buried the body, the judges declared him “innocent for lack of evidence” because in the oral trial, the confession “was not enough,” so despite his self-incrimination he went free. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) sentenced Rubí's murderer but he fled; he never went to jail because the Chihuahua prosecutor's office did not carry out the arrest warrant against him.

For this reason, Marisela Escobedo set herself up in front of the Government Palace of Chihuahua to demand that the governor intervene, but Marisela was murdered in that very spot by an “unknown person” with a shot to the head on December 16, 2010. The government silenced another woman's voice demanding justice.

documentos.index_title: 2017 - ALDA FACIO'S REFLECTIONS ON FACEBOOK, 2017
documentos.index_subtitle: On the denial of the struggle against the diversity of multiple oppressions of 60s-70s feminism.
documentos.title: 2017 - Alda Facio's Reflections on Facebook, 2017
documentos.subtitle: On the denial of the struggle against the diversity of multiple oppressions of 60s-70s feminism by “intersectional feminism.”
paragraphs: Many young women who call themselves “intersectional feminists” claim that 60s and 70s feminism (the so-called “second wave”) ignored the diversity of life and experiences of women, accusing it of being “white feminism.” Alda Facio, as a young woman of color—because being Latin American in the US automatically made her “of color”—was part of the feminism of those decades that actively participated against the Vietnam War and in anti-imperialist and anti-racist movements.

60s and 70s feminism provided great Afro-American feminist thinkers and activists like Audre Lorde, Bell Hooks, and Angela Davis, or the Combahee River Collective composed of black and lesbian women who articulated the concept of multiple oppression, criticizing both sexism and homophobia in the black community and racism and homophobia within the feminist movement. A feminism that fought by organizing against its multiple oppressions, not only against patriarchy but also against capitalism, imperialism, colonialism, consumerism, and for the planet.

Erasing the contributions of women of color, ecofeminists, lesbians, from other nationalities, etc., from the feminist movement before the emergence of “intersectional feminism” is to ignore the contributions of the enormous diversity of women active in those decades. The “new feminisms” that recognize the intersection of oppressions, like that of women with disabilities or indigenous women, cannot ignore these contributions of 60s and 70s color, lesbofeminist, socialist, Marxist, pacifist, hippie, and community feminists.

documentos.index_title: 1979 – THE ADVENTURES OF SUPERLESBI AND ANA PÉREZ
documentos.index_subtitle: Comic strip presenting a positive and powerful image of lesbians.
documentos.title:
1979 – THE ADVENTURES OF SUPERLESBI AND ANA PÉREZ
YAN MARÍA YAOYÓLOTL CASTRO
documentos.subtitle: Comic strip presenting a positive and powerful image of lesbians against denigration, demonization, and patriarchal repression.
paragraphs: Superlesbi is a 1979 comic strip that presents a proactive image of lesbianism, in contrast to the negative, violence-laden, and demonized image disseminated by patriarchal culture, refuting that it was a physical disease, a psychic pathology, or potentially criminal behavior. Lesbianism was women breaking with the role or stereotype of femininity imposed by said patriarchal culture (today wrongly called gender) centered on forced heterosexuality. Heterosexuality understood as the institution through which men directly controlled and subdued women, and femininity as the patriarchal cultural social training used to disable women from developing all their capacities by reducing them to mothers and wives, reproducers of the species, and servants of a man.

The protagonist was Superlesbi in her public life, and in her private life (the closet), her secret personality was Miss Ana Pérez, extremely feminine and apparently heterosexual. This femininity made her appear dependent, fearful, insecure, weak, submissive, and clumsy, contrasting with her true personality as a strong, brave, active, and independent woman, and also powerful since she knew how to fight and combat—a warrior. The warrior that exists within each lesbian, a superwoman inhibited by said sexual stereotype or role of femininity imposed by patriarchal society.

The message was that lesbian women had a Superlesbi within themselves, an internal force they had to discover within their own interior to face patriarchy. Therefore, when they confronted a violent situation, they should close their eyes and establish contact with their inner being, invoking their internal force, and Superlesbi would appear to strengthen them. An interesting fact was that the publication faced sexism, but also patriarchy, imperialism, classism, and racism.

documentos.index_title: 2014 – PATRIARCHY, SEX IS THE ROOT OF OPPRESSION
documentos.index_subtitle: Patriarchy is The System on which all oppressions are based.
documentos.title: 2014 – PATRIARCHY, SEX IS THE ROOT OF OPPRESSION
documentos.subtitle: Patriarchy is The System on which all oppressions, discriminations, and violences experienced by humanity and nature are based.
paragraphs: In this video, Adriana Guzmán, an Aymara q'ewsa* (lesbian) indigenous Bolivian lesbian feminist and member of the Anti-patriarchal Community Feminism organization, explains that patriarchy is not just another system, it is not a product of capitalism, it is not a consequence of colonization—it is The System. All oppressions, discriminations, and violences experienced by humanity and nature are based on it. Patriarchy is historically built on women's bodies, the only thing that can explain capitalist exploitation.

And she asks, where has humanity learned to exploit? and she answers: on women's bodies. Humanity has learned to exploit, and to let itself be exploited, because in every house every day there is a woman performing an enormous amount of work not recognized as work and, therefore, not paid; one lives daily alongside someone who is permanently exploited—there humanity has learned to exploit on women's bodies. Unpaid work that benefits the boss and multinationals, with them keeping the benefit of that unpaid work of women—that is where human exploitation begins.
*Q'ewsa or K'ewsa is an Aymara word for non-heterosexual people, assumed by Aymara lesbians.

documentos.title: 2005 - INDEPENDENT LESBIAN FEMINIST SOCIALISTS (LIFS) OF PERU
documentos.subtitle: The Independent Lesbian Feminist Socialist Collective (LIFS) of Peru has as one of its fundamental objectives to end patriarchy and neoliberalism.
paragraphs: The INDEPENDENT LESBIAN FEMINIST SOCIALIST collective (LIFS) was born in 2005 in Peru. It is a socialist lesbian feminist organization for the promotion and defense of the human rights of women in general and lesbians in particular through revolutionary and creative proposals aimed at eliminating discrimination based on sexual orientation as well as racism, classism, and all forms of violence with the aim of achieving the eradication of patriarchy and the neoliberal model to build a just, plural, and solidary society in Peru and Latin America.

LIFS proposes to deepen a radical democracy that guarantees corporal and sexual autonomy based on a sexual and reproductive revolution; to end the imposition of heterosexuality as the only form of human sexuality and normativity based on oppressive gender roles—in synthesis, against misogyny, lesbophobia, and all forms of repression of eroticism, sexuality, affectivity, and lesbian solidarity. It proposes a socialist lesbian feminist movement to change society and patriarchal and machista relations.

Clarifying note: The brochure reproduced below was distributed in Mexico at a lesbian film-debate event almost three years ago, and since then, we have tried to establish contact with its authors through all possible means—FB, WhatsApp, and phones—and it has never been possible. In the absence of contact and as years passed, we decided to publish the brochure because we have many ideological coincidences with LIFS and because we consider it very important for Mexican lesbians to know its content. Additionally, we prepared a presentation illustrated by ourselves that we hope will one day reach their knowledge and be to their liking, based on acting with the best of intentions. For a socialist feminist revolution.
